solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Liberal policy for each point added to message

indicators.note: added to says the point's word is tacked on after the message's word

parts.note: per means for each, as in 'per head'
a missive is a letter or message
a ness is a headland or point, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Inverness... and Sheerness

explanation.surface: A political party's liberal programme where each new item is bolted onto its manifesto message.
explanation.walkthrough: NESS, a promontory, appears in British place names such as Sheerness and Dungeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Permissiveness is a tolerant, lenient attitude, the hallmark of a liberal regime or approach.

clue.text: Group of artists rebuilt atelier, perhaps

indicators.note: rebuilt means put together again in a new form, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Maybe the painters reconstructed their studio.
explanation.walkthrough: An atelier is an artist's studio, fitting the surface; 'perhaps' looks like a hedge but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood was a Victorian circle of painters including Rossetti, Millais and Hunt.

clue.text: Minister securing a source of power

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the minister holds the letter inside

parts.note: a rector is a parish minister

explanation.surface: A clergyman obtaining a power supply for his parish.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear reactor is a plant generating energy, so it is a source of power.

clue.text: Fill in for medic, somewhat ignorant

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone standing in for a doctor who knows rather little medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ill-informed means lacking knowledge, which is what ignorant describes.

clue.text: Composed second edition, finally put away

indicators.note: finally says the eating word comes at the end

parts.note: to put away food is to eat it, past tense ate

explanation.surface: A second edition was written and then finally shelved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' looks like 'written', fitting the edition, but it means calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedate describes someone calm and unhurried, the same as a composed manner.

clue.text: Opposed to having a large animal inside, beats it

indicators.note: having means containing, so the opposed word holds the rest
inside says the large animal phrase sits within the outer word

parts.note: vs is short for versus, opposed to
a moose is a large deer

explanation.surface: Someone against keeping a big animal indoors, beating it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beats it' is slang for leaves in a hurry, not hitting.
explanation.definitionFit: To vamoose is American slang for to leave quickly, the same as to scram.

clue.text: Juvenile delinquent has it both ways, a pointless achievement

indicators.note: has it both ways says the run is held forwards in one word and backwards in the other

parts.note: the letters sit inside the first word, and backwards inside the second

explanation.surface: A young offender who wants it both ways ends up achieving nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The three letters show forwards in 'juvenile' and backwards in 'delinquent'; either one gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nil is a score of zero, so achieving it means scoring no points at all.

clue.text: Trying to discover what cat can do?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: ..., from the proverb 'a cat may look at a king'

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a cat may look at a king' means even lowly people have rights; read as two words the answer is the cat's privilege.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeking is searching for something, and split up it describes what the proverb allows the cat.

clue.text: Dog in manger perturbed pastor

indicators.note: perturbed means disturbed, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: a pastor is a shepherd of his flock, the word coming from Latin for shepherd

explanation.surface: The nativity scene: a minister upset to find a dog in the manger.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'dog in the manger' is a spiteful person; here the manger is simply the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The German shepherd is a large working breed, also called an Alsatian, used by police.

clue.text: Made possible what's accomplished, in conclusion

indicators.note: in says the accomplished word sits inside the conclusion word

parts.note: the end is the conclusion
an able person is accomplished or skilled

explanation.surface: A statement that skill brought about the final result.
explanation.definitionFit: To enable something is to make it possible, so the past tense matches 'Made possible'.

clue.text: Playwright, to a greater extent, penning fiction

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, as a pen encloses sheep, so the fiction word goes inside

parts.note: more means to a greater extent
a lie is a fiction, an untruth

explanation.surface: A dramatist who writes ever more invented stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' looks like writing, fitting the playwright, but here it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Moliere was the great seventeenth-century French comic dramatist, author of Tartuffe.

clue.text: Skill needed in aircraft-carrier left, right, and centre

indicators.note: centre says the right-hand letter is set in the middle of the other pair
left points to the edges of the first half of the compound, the letters bounding it

parts.note: its two end letters, the leftmost and the one at the compound's centre

indicators.note: right points to the rightmost letter, at the end of the whole compound

parts.note: its last letter

explanation.surface: A skill that is called for all over an aircraft carrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left, right, and centre' reads as 'everywhere', but it takes the leftmost, rightmost and central letters of the fifteen-letter 'aircraft-carrier'; the central one is the T ending 'aircraft'.
explanation.definitionFit: Art in the sense of craft or knack, as in 'the art of persuasion', is a skill.

clue.text: State support, nominal as it might be

indicators.note: might be suggests these letters could become something else when reworked

explanation.surface: A remark that official backing for a country could be purely nominal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nationalism is fervent backing for one's own nation, that is, support for the state.

clue.text: Former Tory leader annoyed, then mad

indicators.note: mad means crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

explanation.surface: A former Conservative leader got irritated, then furious.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was the Conservative British Prime Minister from 1955 to 1957, brought down by the Suez crisis.
explanation.definitionFit: He led the Conservative (Tory) party and the country after Churchill retired in 1955.

clue.text: School that breaks new ground

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., the famous English public school near London
second meaning: a farm implement that breaks up ploughed soil

explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks new ground' sounds like pioneering, praising a progressive school, but it is literal farming.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrow is both a renowned English boarding school and a spiked frame dragged over fields to break clods.

clue.text: Military HQ where sides meet obtusely

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the ..., US Defense Department headquarters
second meaning: a regular five-sided figure has interior angles of 108 degrees, all obtuse

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sides meet obtusely' hints at dim-witted opposing parties in talks, but it is geometry.
explanation.definitionFit: The five-sided building in Virginia housing the US defence department takes its name from the polygon shape.

clue.text: At short notice, put up sordid information on computer

indicators.note: put up in a down clue means written upwards, so read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written
ad is short for advertisement, a notice
base means low, sordid

explanation.surface: Someone quickly publicising grubby details on a computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A database is an organised store of data held in electronic form.

clue.text: English team, say, demolished weak opposition

indicators.note: demolished means knocked down and broken up, so the letters are rebuilt

explanation.surface: A sports report: an English team crushed a feeble opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy meat is an idiom for an opponent or target that is easily beaten or exploited.

clue.text: Somewhat amateurish player's exceptional promise

indicators.note: exceptional reads here as out of the ordinary, so the letters are taken out of order

explanation.surface: A part-time player showing remarkable potential.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-pro is a sportsman paid for playing but not full-time, so partly amateur.

clue.text: River in Scotland, from what we hear? Dee is that

indicators.note: from what we hear means the river's name is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: the Forth flows past Stirling into the Firth of Forth at Edinburgh

explanation.surface: Musing about Scottish rivers: the Dee is one too, from what people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Dee looks like the Scottish river Aberdeen stands on, but it is the letter D, fourth in the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: D comes in the fourth position of the alphabet, so the letter's spoken name is that ordinal.

clue.text: Copy page in souvenir article

indicators.note: in says the page letter is placed within the souvenir

parts.note: a relic is a keepsake or souvenir
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A collector copying a page from a souvenir booklet.
explanation.definitionFit: A replica is an exact reproduction of something, a copy.

clue.text: Spiritual teaching in religious group is not revealed

indicators.note: in places the teaching inside the group

parts.note: a sect is a religious group
RE is religious education, a school subject in Britain

explanation.surface: A cult's doctrines kept hidden from outsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: RE stands for religious education, the subject taught in British schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Something secret is kept hidden, unknown to others.

clue.text: Frantically edit my e-mail, without delay

indicators.note: frantically means in a wild, disordered way, so the letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: A panicked office worker rushing to fix an email before sending it.
explanation.definitionFit: Immediately means at once, instantly, with no pause or wait.

clue.text: Pressure mounted for young boxer, say

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
mounted means up, as on a horse

explanation.surface: A trainer piling pressure on a young fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxer is the dog breed, not a fighter.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer is a dog breed, and a young dog is a pup; 'say' marks it as one example.

clue.text: Display work the writer put back in stores

indicators.note: put back says the whole string is turned to run the other way

parts.note: to air something is to display it
op is short for opus, a work
the writer refers to the setter, me

explanation.surface: A shop window display that the author returned to its store.
explanation.definitionFit: Emporia is the plural of emporium, a large shop or store.

clue.text: Released on bail, heads off to commit a crime

indicators.note: heads off means taking the leading letters off each of the next words

explanation.surface: A suspect freed on bail who promptly goes out to offend again.
explanation.definitionFit: Robbery is a crime, so to rob is to commit one.

clue.text: Revolutionary warship's first spotted in European port, possibly

parts.note: a red is a revolutionary, a communist

indicators.note: first selects the opening letter of the warship word

parts.note: first letter of warship

explanation.surface: A rebel warship sighted in a port somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' seems to be a harbour, but it is the fortified wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a fortified red wine from Portugal, so it is one example.

clue.text: Principle partially applied to fold flag

parts.note: to double something is to fold it over
a standard is a flag or banner

explanation.surface: A rule only half-enforced when lowering and folding a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: A double standard is a rule applied unequally, strictly to some people but leniently to others.
